### Today we will be talking about mapping functions.

Let's begin by loading some libraries:

(maps, mapdata, and mapproj are new!)

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
#library(rsconnect) # maybe no need
library(maps)
library(mapdata)

```


---

### Outline

Today we will be working with Maps!

specifically the {maps} function
and the {sf} function

---

### Part one: Package overview

{maps} is the package we will use today. Very simple

{sf} and {rnaturalearth} are more complicated and fancy map packages for people who love making fancy maps

{maptiles} for the online lecture (uses satellite data)

{leaflet} interactive maps

{tmap} more interactive maps

{ggmap} the kind of free trial that requires a credit card

---

### Load in Data

```{r}

# Population in California by county
popdata <- read_csv(here("Week_07", "Data", "CApopdata.csv"))

# Seastar counts at field sites in California
stars <- read_csv(here("Week_07", "Data", "stars.csv"))

```
### Make a new dataframe

```{r}

world <- map_data("world")

head(world)


```

### Can also do this with countries:

```{r}
usa <- map_data("usa")

head(usa)

```

### Can also call "state" or "county"

```{r}
states <- map_data("state")

head(states)
```

```{r}
counties <- map_data("county")

head(counties)
```


These will pull all the data for the states and counties in the (mainland) US.

---

### Structure of the data

long - longitude

lat - latitude

order - the order in which ggplot connects the dots

region/subregion - the region or subregion a set of points surrounds

group - THIS ONE IS IMPORTANT : control whether the points next to each other are connected or not. Points in the same group get connected, different groups cause ggplot to "lift the pen"

### Donʻt forget group = group!!!

---

# ok make a basic map time!

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group))
```

Nice, alright

---

### But why are the aesthetics inside of the geom_polygon instead of the ggplot?

Because we want them to be separate from ALL plots, we only want it to apply to the polygon plot.

### More details

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = region),
               color = "black") +
  guides(fill = "none") +   # Make sure to remove the guide or else we will have SO MUCH Legend that there is no map
  theme_minimal() +         # Make the theme minimal!
  theme(panel.background =
          element_rect(fill = "lightblue")) +   # make the ocean blue!
  coord_map(projection = "sinusoidal",   # change the projection
            xlim = c(-180, 180))
```

ok add california map data:

```{r}

CA_data <- states |> 
  filter(region == "california")

```



Challenge: Make a simple map of california!

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CA_data,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = region))   # no need to do this, but just wanted to see what it'd look like
```



Messing around with counties:

```{r}

# extract california counties data
CA_county_data <- counties |> 
  filter(region == "california")


CA_county_state <- inner_join(CA_county_data, CA_data, by = "region")



```

Whoops I really messed up the join and now have a bunch of .x/.y's


OK let's try again to add counties:

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CA_county_state,
               color = "black",
               aes(x = long.x, y = lat.x,
                   group = group.x,
                   fill = subregion.x)) +
  labs(title = "Map of California",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude")+
  coord_map(projection = "mercator")+
  theme_void()
```

Ok next up: add multiple layers of data

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CA_data,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group),
               color = "black") +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void()
```


First thing is we will inner_join population with county data

```{r}
CApop_county <- popdata |>
  select("subregion" = County, Population) |>   # rename to match counties
  inner_join(counties) |>
  filter(region == "california")                 # some county names repeat in other states


head(CApop_county)
```


Make a map using all of the pop data:

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CApop_county,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = Population),
               color = "black") +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gradient(transform = "log10")
```

What if we had some sea star data we wanted to slap on the map?

```{r}
head(stars)
```


```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CApop_county,
               aes(x = long, 
                   y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = Population),
               color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = stars,
             aes(x = long,
                 y = lat,
                 size = star_no),
             shape = 18) +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gradient(transform = "log10") +
  labs(size = "# stars/m²")


ggsave(here("Week_07", "Output", "CApop.pdf"))
```

### Ok that was fun!

Now time for a brief overview of {sf} + {rnaturalearth}

{sf} stands for simple features and is the current standard for spatial data

- spatial objects are just dataframes, all tidyverse verbs work on them

- handles projections, CRS transformations, spatial joins natively

- no need to manage group manually!

---

Let's give {sf} a shot

```{r}

library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rnaturalearthdata)

world_sf <- ne_countries(scale = "medium",    # get the data
                         returnclass = "sf")

ggplot(world_sf) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgray",    # plot the data
          color = "white") +
  theme_void()
```

Nice! 

```{r}

ggplot(world_sf) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgray", color = "white") +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") + # Robinson projection
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Robinson Projection")


```
